content: Griseofulvin is a medication used to treat fungal infections of the skin, hair, and nails that do not respond to topical treatments like creams or lotions. By inhibiting fungal growth, it helps alleviate symptoms such as itching, redness, peeling, scaly skin, and discolored nails. How to Use: Shake the bottle well before each dose. Take this medication orally as directed by your doctor. For optimal absorption, it is best taken with or after a meal containing a moderate amount of fat. The dosage is determined based on your medical condition and response to treatment. For children, the dosage is also based on weight. The duration of treatment depends on the type of infection. It may take several weeks to months to complete treatment for infections of the scalp, feet, or body. To maintain consistent levels of the medication in your body, take it at evenly spaced intervals and continue for the full prescribed duration, even if symptoms improve after a few days. Side Effects: Common side effects include headache, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, stomach upset, tiredness, dizziness, and trouble sleeping. Prolonged or repeated use may lead to oral thrush or a new vaginal yeast infection. Rare but serious allergic reactions may occur. Symptoms of a severe allergic reaction include rash, itching/swelling (especially of the face/tongue/throat), severe dizziness, and trouble breathing. This medication may cause photosensitivity, so limit sun exposure and use sunscreen or protective clothing when outdoors. Precautions: Inform your doctor if you are allergic to griseofulvin or have any other allergies. This medication may cause dizziness or impair alertness. Avoid alcohol or marijuana, as they can exacerbate these effects. Avoid driving or operating machinery until you are sure you can do so safely. Alcohol consumption during treatment may cause flushing and a rapid heartbeat. Griseofulvin may harm an unborn baby. Women should avoid becoming pregnant while using this medication and for one month after the last dose. Reliable birth control methods should be used. The effects of this drug on human sperm are unknown, but animal studies suggest potential risks. Men should consult their doctor about waiting a period of time after treatment before fathering a child. Drug Interactions: Griseofulvin may interact with other medications, altering their effectiveness or increasing the risk of side effects. It can reduce the effectiveness of hormonal birth control methods, potentially leading to pregnancy. Discuss alternative or backup birth control methods with your doctor. Keep a list of all medications and supplements you are taking and share it with your healthcare provider. Overdose: In case of overdose, seek immediate medical attention. In the U.S., call 911 or the Poison Control Center at 1-800-222-1222. Storage: Store at room temperature, away from light and moisture. Do not store in the bathroom. Properly discard expired or unused medication. Monitoring: Patients on prolonged therapy should undergo periodic monitoring of organ function, including renal, hepatic, and hematopoietic systems. Discontinue use if severe skin reactions (e.g., Stevens-Johnson syndrome, toxic epidermal necrolysis) or jaundice occur. Pregnancy and Lactation: Griseofulvin is classified as pregnancy category X due to evidence of embryotoxic and teratogenic effects in animal studies. It should not be used during pregnancy. It is unknown if the drug passes into breast milk. Due to potential tumorigenicity, breastfeeding is not recommended while using this medication. Additional Information: This medication is extensively metabolized by the liver, primarily via the CYP3A4 enzyme, and has a half-life of 9-22 hours. It is excreted in urine (less than 1% as unchanged drug), feces, and perspiration. Always consult your healthcare provider for complete information tailored to your specific health needs.
